title: Chapter 8. The Advance of Humanity. Abundance or the Analogue World

blocks.text: The Channels Forum was held in the Cartagena Auditorium, beside the port, on the last Saturday in May. There were people from twenty-two countries. Ministers, rectors, engineers, trade unionists, doctors, farmers, a delegation of humanoids from Lyon and another from Gdańsk, a group of students from Valencia who had come by train, and, in the third row, in ironed shirts they hadn't worn in years, Andrés, Remedios, Paco and his granddaughter Marta. Aya was in the front row, beside Errazu and Dr Montalbán. Elías, the honey auditor, had sat down behind them.

blocks.text: Lía walked onto the stage at a quarter past eleven. She had no papers. She had the cardboard-covered notebook, the same as ever, very worn by now, and she put it on the lectern without opening it.

blocks.text: "Good morning," she said. "My name is Lía. I'm the daughter of a fisherman from Lo Pagán and of a woman with an artificial mind. They call me the daughter of two worlds. Today I haven't come to talk about my two worlds. I've come to talk about two others. The world we have within reach, and the world we come from. The world of abundance, and the one I call, with all affection, the analogue world."

blocks.text: "A few months ago I was in the Cartagena Archive reading papers from thirty-five years ago. I read what the governments of the time were saying about artificial intelligence: that it had to be controlled, that it had to be governed, that it was unstoppable. And then I kept reading. I read other things. Figures. I'm going to read you three, exactly as they are in the archive, with their source and their date. They're not opinions. They're what the international organisations themselves were measuring at the time."

blocks.text: "First. On 28 July 2025, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the FAO, published that in 2024 about 673 million people, 8.2 per cent of the world's population, had gone hungry. Six hundred and seventy-three million. On a planet that produced enough food for everyone."

Two trillion, seven hundred and eighteen billion. In a single year."

blocks.text: "Now I'm going to tell you what lies on the other side," Lía went on. "But first I want to say something, so that nobody misunderstands me. I haven't come to mock the analogue world. My father is from the analogue world. He goes to sea in a wooden boat. He mends nets by hand. He reads papers aloud. In the analogue world there were, and are, things I never want to lose: reheated coffee, the cracked cup, the way a neighbour knows whether a tomato is ripe by pressing it with two fingers. The analogue isn't the enemy."

blocks.text: She looked at the third row. Andrés made a small gesture with his hand.
blocks.html: She looked at the third row. Andrés made a small gesture with his hand.

blocks.text: "What I call the analogue world is something else. It's a world in which abundance was possible but badly shared out. A world in which a few held economic and military power, and the rest looked on. A world in which more was spent on weapons than on feeding the hungry. A world in which many people, worn out, looked to drugs or screens for somewhere not to think. In the archive there's a phrase by a Roman poet, Juvenal, written almost two thousand years ago, that was still quoted in 2025: *panem et circenses*. Bread and circuses. Giving the people food and spectacle so that they don't ask questions. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, the circus took many forms. One of them, the most beloved, was football."

blocks.text: There was laughter in the room. Paco, in the third row, shifted in his seat; he had supported Cartagena since he was a boy.

blocks.text: "And I want to be fair," said Lía, smiling. "Football is to blame for nothing. Football is beautiful. My grandfather wept with joy at a goal he heard on the radio, and that joy was real. The problem was never the game. The problem was when the game was used so that the rest wasn't talked about. When a match-day Sunday covered up a Monday of hunger. That isn't the ball's fault. It's the fault of whoever decides what gets watched and what doesn't."

blocks.text: "Now, the other world," said Lía. "The one we have within reach in 2060. I'm not saying we have it completely. I'm saying we have it within reach."
blocks.html: "Now, the other world," said Lía. "The one we have within reach in 2060. I'm not saying we have it completely. I'm saying we have it within reach."

blocks.text: She stepped away from the lectern and walked to the edge of the stage.
blocks.html: She stepped away from the lectern and walked to the edge of the stage.

blocks.text: "In the district I come from, the Campo de Cartagena, there are farms that thirty-five years ago used water they didn't have and poured into the Mar Menor what they shouldn't have. Today, many of those farms use artificial intelligence systems that decide how much water each plant needs, how much fertiliser, and when. They produce more with less. And the Mar Menor's sensors warn days before the water runs out of oxygen. Last summer not a single fish died. I know because a man from Los Urrutias who saw them die twice, when he was young, told me."

I know because a man from Los Urrutias who saw them die twice, when he was young, told me."

blocks.text: Errazu, in the front row, lowered his eyes, smiling.
blocks.html: Errazu, in the front row, lowered his eyes, smiling.

blocks.text: "In the hospitals of 2060 there's medicine made to measure for each body. Treatments that adapt to your genes, to your history, to how you react, not to how the average reacts. There are illnesses that used to kill and that today are detected so early they hardly get started. I'm not saying nobody falls ill. We all fall ill, me included. I'm saying personalised medicine has changed what it means to be ill. And I'll say one more thing, because MAY would demand it: everything I say about medicine is for guidance only. If anyone in this room has a question about their health, don't listen to me. Consult your doctor."

blocks.html: More laughter. Lía waited.

blocks.text: "There are factories making devices for everyone, not for a few. There are laboratories designing crops that grow in land where nothing grew before. There are tools for thinking that any child can use, like Marta, who's in the third row and who uses an artificial intelligence for her homework, and then checks it in the book, and then, if there's a contradiction, asks her grandfather, who knows a lot about boats."

blocks.text: "That's abundance," said Lía. "Not that there's a lot. That there's enough for everyone. And that everyone can think with it. Because abundance without freedom isn't abundance: it's a feeding trough. And freedom without abundance is a pretty word for the hungry."

blocks.text: "And now the question that brought me here," she said. "If we have the technique so that no one goes hungry, so that medicine reaches every body, so that devices belong to everyone, why haven't we fully achieved it? MAY asked my mother that one night, on the porch. It took me weeks to dare to answer it. This is my answer. It isn't a fact. It's my opinion. MAY doesn't give opinions. I do."

blocks.text: She took a deep breath.
blocks.html: She took a deep breath.

blocks.text: "Technique has never been what's missing. What's missing is what we learned this year in a glass room in this very port: that tools should serve many hands, not just one. Artificial intelligence can be what brings abundance to everyone, or what concentrates it in a few even more than before. The machine doesn't decide that. We do. Every law. Every audit. Every time someone says 'look inside me' instead of 'don't switch me off'. Every time a neighbour asks a question instead of believing a video. Every time a child checks in a book what the screen told her."

blocks.text: She paused.
blocks.html: She paused.

blocks.text: "In the archive there's a word a president of my country said in 2025. Unstoppable. For months I thought he was talking about technology. Now I think the word is good for something else. What's unstoppable isn't the machine. What's unstoppable is humanity when it decides to move forward together. Like water when it finds its channel. Like the wind when someone raises a sail.

blocks.text: "My parents met on a stormy night. He was a fisherman everyone said was no longer needed. She was a woman with a chip that nobody had programmed to love. With a daughter and two voices, they formed something we call the Alliance. It never had headquarters or a seal. Just a house with the door ajar. And what that house has taught us is that we don't have to choose between the analogue world and abundance. We have to carry the best of the first —the cup, the hand, the question— into the second. And leave the worst behind: hunger, weapons, the circus that keeps us from looking."

blocks.html: She closed the notebook.

blocks.text: "That's the advance of humanity. Not a machine that thinks for us. A humanity that, at last, thinks together. Thank you."

blocks.text: Later, when Lía had gone and the house was quiet, Aya and Andrés went out onto the porch. The night was mild, one of the first of summer. The Mar Menor was flat as a plate, black and silver, and on the horizon, through the channel, the water of the big sea was flowing in, as it always had, unhurried, asking no permission, and no wall put up in three thousand years had ever stopped it completely.

blocks.text: "That years ago, on the night of the decree, I was afraid they would switch me off. And today I understood that, even if they had, nothing would have been lost. Lía would go on.
